::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Where is the mistake that I'm making regarding a trivial solution in this simple two-equation math problem?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/5131658/where-is-the-mistake-that-im-making-regarding-a-trivial-solution-in-this-simple), asked by [Xukrao](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/1733552/xukrao) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2026-04-05; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> My high school math seems to be more more rusty than I thought. I have been trying my hand at the following simple math textbook problem:
>
> > Given are the functions $f(x)=x^2-x$ and $g(x)=p/x$. Find the values
> > of $x$ of $p$ corresponding to a point where both functions intersect
> > each other perpendicularly.
>
> To solve this problem I started with the equations $f(x)=g(x)$ and $f'(x) \cdot g'(x)=-1$. These can be expanded I believe to $p=x^3-x^2$ and $p=x^2/(2x-1)$.
>
> Subsequently equating these two expressions for $p$ gives me two solutions for $x$, namely $x=0$ and $x=3/2$. These in turn give me two corresponding solutions for $p$, namely $p=0$ and $p=9/8$.
>
> The solution $x=3/2$ with $p=9/8$ matches the one given in the solution manual. However the found trivial solution $x=0$ with $p=0$ that I also have is not in the solution manual, nor does plotting the functions graphically with $p=0$ show an intersection where the functions curves are actually perpendicular.
>
> So it seems clear that I've made a mistake somewhere or are overlooking something obvious with regard to this found trivial solution. But where exactly? What am I still missing here?
:::

Fun question, and nice solution. When you cleared the denominators from $x^2-x = p/x$ to get $x^3 - x^2 = p$, you introduced the possibility of $x=0$ as a solution. Similarly with $(2x-1)\left(-\frac{p}{x^2}\right)=-1$. But since $g$ is not defined at $0$, the extra solution should be discarded.
